prompt: A client's link sends 1,500-byte frames, each taking about 17 µs of data airtime, and every channel access costs about 200 µs of fixed overhead (DIFS, backoff, preamble, SIFS, acknowledgment). Throughput is poor. Which change would raise throughput the most?

options.text: Double the PHY rate, so each frame takes about 8.5 µs
options.explanation: Doubling the rate shrinks only the 17 µs data part of a roughly 217 µs access. The 200 µs overhead still dominates, so throughput rises by only a few per cent.

options.text: Aggregate about 32 frames into each channel access with a Block Ack
options.explanation: Correct. The 200 µs overhead is now paid once for about 544 µs of data, so the share of airtime carrying data rises from about 8% to roughly 73%.

options.text: Lengthen DIFS so collisions are less likely
options.explanation: A longer fixed gap adds overhead to every access. It does not address the fact that each access carries very little data.

options.text: Send each frame twice so lost frames need no retransmission
options.explanation: Duplicating frames doubles the airtime used per byte delivered. The fixed overhead is still paid for every access.

workedExample:
1. Compare the two parts of one access: about 17 µs of data and about 200 µs of fixed overhead. Overhead is over 90% of the airtime.
2. A faster PHY rate shrinks only the data part. Even halving 17 µs leaves the access at about 208 µs, so the delivered rate barely changes.
3. Aggregation keeps the overhead fixed but fills the access with more data. With 32 frames, about 544 µs of data shares the same 200 µs overhead: roughly 73% efficiency instead of about 8%.
4. So when per-access overhead dominates, sending more per access beats sending each frame faster. Real overhead also includes per-frame delimiters and padding, and aggregation needs enough queued data for the same receiver.
